bridges.mechanism: Reduced availability of commercial satellite bandwidth and coverage impairs vessel tracking, logistics coordination and insurance assessments for bulk energy shipments, increasing uncertainty about delivery timings and thus short- to medium-term price dispersion.

Reductions or disruptions in commercial satellite communications availability increase uncertainty in logistics, commodity flows and market information, producing greater short-term volatility in key asset prices and exchange rates.

Visible government pressure on private communications providers to censor or alter services erodes public perceptions of institutional independence and fairness, causing a measurable drop in aggregate trust in core institutions.

Visible government pressure on private comms providers to alter services in the Ukraine war normalizes and politicizes national-security interventions in commercial tech, prompting regulators to open investigations, tighten reporting requirements and broaden oversight of AI firms and cross‑border data/chip flows tied to the US–China rivalry.

Demonstrated reliance of military operations on commercial satellite and comms elevates dual‑use concerns among legislators and regulators, triggering tighter export controls, compliance audits and sector‑specific oversight focused on AI and associated suppliers in the US–China rivalry.

Active technical or policy restrictions on commercial satellite communications degrade remote monitoring, control and automated safety systems for pipelines, LNG facilities and offshore platforms, directly raising the likelihood of operational failures and temporary supply interruptions.

Increased technical and policy restrictions (throttling, geofencing, access cuts) directly interrupt transnational information and financial flows, reducing the strength and speed of political and informational shock transmission across borders.

When commercial satcom services are actively restricted (by providers or states) in the Russia–Ukraine theatre, non-state Iranian-aligned actors that rely on the same global commercial links lose real-time command, targeting and guidance, materially reducing their ability and frequency to mount long-range cross-border strikes.

Increased susceptibility of communications channels to jamming, spoofing or false signals produces spurious outage reports and ambiguous market intelligence, prompting abrupt trading reactions and larger short-term swings in energy prices.

High-profile jamming, spoofing or interception incidents raise perceived operational and geopolitical risk among investors for firms and markets exposed to the theatre, lowering aggregate risk appetite and sentiment.

Exposed and exploited information-security weaknesses (spoofing, jamming, comms capture) demonstrated in the Russia–Ukraine war are adopted and adapted by Iranian forces and proxies, improving their ability to degrade adversary sensors and navigation and thereby increasing successful cross‑border strike rates.

High-profile interceptions, spoofing or compromise of communications used in the conflict demonstrate exploitation pathways for AI services and cloud infrastructure, leading investors to downgrade risk appetite for AI startups and projects that rely on exposed commercial comms or insecure supply chains.

Escalating regional hostilities raise geopolitical uncertainty and prompt portfolio reallocations toward safe assets, reducing aggregate investor willingness to hold riskier energy and commodity exposures.

Sharp increases in regional fighting produce high-casualty incidents and intense media coverage that mobilize local populations and diasporas into immediate demonstrations for or against government policy and military action.

Escalating regional conflict raises operational, insurance and legal risk for commercial providers, causing them to proactively implement technical restrictions (geofencing, beam shutdowns, bandwidth curtailment) over broader regions, which increases the intensity and scope of service restrictions affecting users in the Russia–Ukraine war zone.

Sustained escalation in regional conflicts increases geopolitical tail‑risk perceptions among global asset managers and VC funds, causing a measurable pullback in willingness to accept valuation and operational risk in internationally linked AI investments.

More frequent cross-border missile and drone strikes that target or threaten export terminals, pipelines and shipping lanes increase the assessed probability and expected magnitude of near-term physical supply interruptions for energy commodities.

Frequent cross-border strikes force neighbouring states and international institutions to issue rapid political/security responses and warnings, accelerating the speed and reach of shock transmission across borders.

Higher frequency of cross-border strikes increases the probability of direct damage to or operational evacuation of satellite ground infrastructure (earth stations, uplink/downlink facilities) and forces providers to suspend beams over contested airspace, reducing commercial satellite communications availability in theatres relevant to the Russia–Ukraine war.

A spike in cross‑border strikes tied to actors perceived as backed by regional adversaries accelerates national‑security framing in Washington and allied capitals, triggering faster, broader regulatory and export‑control reviews of AI development and cross‑border tech ties.

Sustained upward moves in oil prices quickly raise domestic fuel and transportation costs, provoking street-level economic grievances that increase the size and spread of protests over weeks to months.
An increased supply disruption risk premium is directly incorporated into bids and futures pricing, raising the market-clearing price for energy commodities above baseline supply-demand fundamentals.
Rising risk premia on energy supply elevate perceived geopolitical and market risk, prompting portfolio reallocation toward safe assets and a contemporaneous deterioration in investor risk appetite.

A higher energy disruption risk premium raises operational energy costs for large-scale training and inference fleets, squeezing margins and causing cloud and AI service providers to slow capacity expansion and thus reduce near‑term revenue growth.

Direct interdictions, reroutings and delays of tankers and LNG carriers create large, inconsistent shortfalls and timing uncertainty in deliveries that force rapid rebalancing in spot markets and widen price dispersion and realized volatility.

Disruptions to maritime logistics delay delivery of military-grade communications terminals and bespoke SATCOM hardware to Ukraine and its partners, leading frontline forces to rely more heavily on immediately available commercial satellite communications for command, control and ISR.

Acute increases in maritime disruptions delay and raise the cost of delivering specialised AI hardware (GPUs, networking gear) from East Asian manufacturers, prompting lead investors and syndicates to pause or downsize rounds for compute‑heavy AI startups faced with immediate supply constraints.

Rapid AI revenue expansion accelerates cloud and data-center buildout and compute consumption, increasing electricity and fuel demand in key regions and putting upward pressure on aggregate energy price levels.

Faster AI revenue growth enables providers to commercialize AI-based compression, beamforming and link-management tools and to subsidize rollout with satellite operators, increasing effective bandwidth and service availability in the theatre.

Increases in cross-border capital raising for AI firms ease liquidity constraints and information gaps, reducing short-term repricing and bid-ask swings; conversely drops in capital flow driven by rivalry-driven barriers raise market volatility.

A rise in investor willingness to accept geopolitical and sectoral risk amid US–China rivalry directly improves aggregate investor sentiment by supporting higher valuations, risk-on positioning and more favorable market narratives.

A rise in high-profile AI safety incidents attributed to companies or systems linked with one rival state becomes a mobilizing grievance (safety, jobs, national security) that opposition groups and media leverage to organize larger, more frequent public demonstrations.

An uptick in AI safety incidents reveals exploitable flaws in AI components used for network routing, authentication or signal processing, which adversaries can probe or spoof, raising the vulnerability of information flows in the conflict zone.

Escalating AI-related export controls and compliance enforcement drive onshoring and stockpiling of critical chips and associated metals and inputs, producing localized bottlenecks and raising assessed supply-disruption risk for energy- and metals-related commodity chains.

Higher regulatory scrutiny tied to US–China rivalry (export controls, sanctions, enforcement actions) generates immediate transnational alerts and countermeasures that propagate through diplomatic channels, supply chains and financial markets, increasing the speed and strength of cross-border shock transmission.

Escalating regulatory scrutiny of AI vendors tied to US–China rivalry generates additional formal and informal government demands on commercial communications providers (compliance checks, export-control enforcement, data-localization orders) relevant to the Russia–Ukraine theatre.

Regulatory bans or compliance burdens on specific AI/telemetry software and foreign vendors implicated by US–China rivalry cause satellite operators or their software suppliers to disable features or withdraw services in contested regions, reducing available commercial satcom capacity.
Sustained increases in energy prices raise household fuel and transport costs and pressure subsidy budgets, prompting rapid, large-scale demonstrations and strikes by affected constituencies.

Sustained higher global energy prices increase export revenue and hard-currency access for Iran and allied nonstate actors, enabling larger arms purchases, logistics and stipend flows that raise the tempo and severity of regional military operations.

Sustained higher energy prices raise operators' operational and transport costs, prompting commercial providers to curtail, throttle or geofence expensive routes and customers in marginal/conflict areas to contain expenses.

Sustained elevated energy prices raise the marginal cost of compute and data-centre operations, forcing higher customer prices or margin compression that slows revenue growth for large commercial AI providers.

Sharp swings in energy prices force frequent revaluation of energy-linked corporate earnings and hedging positions, driving higher short-term volatility across equities, bonds and FX as markets rebalance.

Sharp short-term swings in energy prices increase incentives for state and proxy actors to conduct demonstrative or coercive cross-border strikes (against shipping, facilities or bases) to influence market sentiment or signal resolve, raising strike frequency.

Acute volatility in energy prices induces a market-wide risk-off, tightens liquidity and underwriting terms, and prompts investors to delay or withdraw from new equity/debt deals, immediately reducing capital raising for AI developers.

A decline in investor risk appetite reduces capital for upstream energy projects and raises insurance/finance costs for shipping and infrastructure, which markets translate into a higher energy supply-disruption risk premium.

A decline in investor appetite reduces capital available for satellite launches, constellation maintenance and capacity expansion, causing delays or cuts in commercial satcom coverage and throughput in the conflict theatre.

Material risks to commodity supplies trigger export controls, rerouting of trade and emergency diplomacy that rapidly transmit political and economic shocks and signals across neighboring and linked states.

Persistent or visible failures to secure key commodity supplies undermine public perceptions of government competence and regulatory capacity, eroding trust in core institutions over subsequent months.

Rising assessed commodity supply-disruption risk prompts shipping companies, insurers and naval actors to reroute, delay or interdict voyages and for states to escalate maritime interdiction/escorting operations, directly increasing the observed rate of seaborne transport disruptions.

Disruptions in energy and critical metal supplies constrain manufacturing, launch cadence and ground‑station upkeep for commercial satcom providers, reducing available bandwidth and coverage in the theatre.

Rising risk of supply disruptions for energy and critical materials drives governments to expand national-security reviews, tighten export controls and foreign-investment screening, increasing regulatory oversight of AI firms and their supply chains.

Large, sustained protests physically block or disable extraction, processing and transport infrastructure (ports, pipelines, refineries) and trigger labor stoppages, directly increasing the assessed probability and magnitude of supply disruptions.

Large-scale protests in neighboring states degrade local security posture and tie down government forces, creating permissive windows that Iranian-aligned militias exploit to increase the frequency of cross‑border strikes.

Spikes in asset-price volatility trigger margin calls and rapid portfolio rebalancing that force large, abrupt flows into or out of energy futures and physical markets, amplifying realized and implied energy price volatility.

Spikes in asset-price volatility cause operators and service providers to defer nonessential expenditures and staffing, degrading patching, monitoring and resilience measures and increasing susceptibility of commercial comms to interception, spoofing or jamming.

Spikes in asset-price volatility raise the effective cost of capital and close IPO/secondary windows, causing venture and public capital-raising for AI firms to pause or shrink until markets stabilize.

Deteriorating investor risk sentiment tied to geopolitical realignment causes traders and funds to widen risk premia on energy contracts, directly raising the market component priced as disruption risk for supply chains in the region.

Improved investor risk sentiment lowers financing costs and unlocks capital for satellite launches, ground infrastructure and capacity leases, increasing available commercial satcom bandwidth and coverage serving the theatre.

An improvement (or deterioration) in investor risk sentiment directly changes portfolio allocations for AI sectors—better sentiment causes allocators to accept higher valuation and operational risk in AI investments while worse sentiment causes immediate de-risking.

Faster and stronger cross-border transmission of political and regulatory shocks (sanctions, export controls, border closures) causes secondary supplier interruptions and logistical cascades that raise commodity supply disruption risk.

Faster, stronger cross-border signal transmission (communications, targeting data and logistics channels) directly enables Iranian command-and-control and proxy networks to coordinate and time more frequent long‑range strikes across borders.

Enhanced cross‑border signalling accelerates coordination of maritime harassment, interdiction and information operations by state and proxy actors (targeting routes, flag states or ports), directly increasing rates of seaborne transport disruption.

Faster and stronger cross-border transmission of political information and coordination prompts states to implement targeted technical and policy restrictions (throttling, geofencing, targeted shutdowns) to blunt spillovers into the Russia–Ukraine theatre.

Faster and stronger cross-border transmission of political, information or financial shocks leads governments to impose export controls, data/localization rules and additional compliance checks on cross-border AI activity, increasing regulatory scrutiny.

A marked decline in institutional trust precipitates policy paralysis, regulatory flip-flops or elevated risk of resource seizures that reduce effective supply or add a sustained risk premium, lifting energy price levels.

Declines in public trust in institutions incentivize governments to exert more formal and informal pressure on private communications providers to control narratives and limit disruptive content related to the conflict.

Falling institutional trust prompts legislators and regulators to open investigations and introduce tighter oversight of prominent AI developers to restore public confidence, whereas rising trust reduces political pressure for new scrutiny.

nodes.label: Starlink access as a lever in the Ukraine war
Commercial satellite communications access
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate level of bandwidth, coverage and service availability provided by commercial satellite communications to users in the theatre.

nodes.label: Provider operational autonomy
nodes.description: Measures the degree to which private communications providers independently set and enforce operational service policies without external direction.

nodes.label: Governmental pressure on providers
nodes.description: Measures the intensity and frequency of formal and informal governmental requests, demands or pressures directed at private communications providers to alter services.

nodes.label: Military dependency on commercial comms
nodes.description: Measures the extent to which military operations rely on commercial satellite and related communications for command, control, ISR and logistics.

nodes.label: Availability of alternative communications
nodes.description: Measures the capacity, readiness and deployability of non-primary communications options (military, terrestrial, or other commercial suppliers) that can substitute disrupted services.

nodes.label: Service restriction intensity
nodes.description: Measures the degree and scope of active technical or policy restrictions applied to commercial communications services (e.g., throttling, geofencing, access cuts).

nodes.label: Military operational effectiveness
nodes.description: Measures the overall effectiveness of military missions and tactical outcomes as influenced by communications, logistics and situational awareness.

nodes.label: Civilian connectivity level
nodes.description: Measures the proportion of the civilian population with reliable access to internet and communications services in the affected area.

nodes.label: Diplomatic tension level
nodes.description: Measures the intensity of diplomatic disputes and bilateral friction arising from contestation over communications services and related policies.

nodes.label: Public perception of private tech power
nodes.description: Measures public and political sentiment about the influence and control that private technology actors have over critical infrastructure and conflict outcomes.

nodes.label: Logistics and infrastructure resilience
nodes.description: Measures the robustness of supply chains, transport nodes and civilian infrastructure to disruptions in communications and associated attacks.

nodes.label: Information-flow security vulnerability
nodes.description: Measures the susceptibility of communications channels to interception, spoofing, jamming or other compromise that degrades information integrity.

nodes.label: Regulatory constraint strength
nodes.description: Measures the scope and enforceability of legal and regulatory frameworks governing private communications providers' operations and state interactions.

nodes.label: International support cohesion
nodes.description: Measures the degree of coordination, policy alignment and resource-sharing among external supporters that affect access to communications and related capabilities.

nodes.label: Battlefield maneuver flexibility
nodes.description: Measures the ability of forces to change tactics, reposition assets and exploit opportunities rapidly, as enabled by communications and situational awareness.

nodes.label: Civilian morale and social resilience
nodes.description: Measures societal cohesion, morale and the capacity of communities to maintain normal functions under communications disruptions and conflict stressors.

Regional conflict intensity
nodes.description: The aggregated severity and tempo of hostile military interactions across the region, measured continuously by incident severity, casualty estimates and operational scope.

nodes.label: Proxy attack rate
nodes.description: The rate at which non-state aligned armed actors conduct offensive operations (raids, strikes, sabotage) per unit time.

nodes.label: Cross-border strike frequency
nodes.description: The frequency of missile, drone and other long-range strikes that traverse international boundaries per unit time.

nodes.label: Military deployment and readiness level
nodes.description: The aggregate posture and mobilization level of armed forces in the theater, including deployment density and alert status.

nodes.label: Diplomatic mediation activity
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of formal and informal mediation efforts, negotiations and shuttle diplomacy taking place per unit time.

nodes.label: De‑escalation signal strength
nodes.description: The perceived strength and credibility of signals and actions indicating reductions in hostilities or commitments to restraint.

nodes.label: Oil price level
nodes.description: The prevailing market price per barrel for benchmark crude as a continuous market state.

nodes.label: Oil price volatility
nodes.description: The short- and medium-term variability of oil prices, measured by realized or implied volatility over a rolling horizon.

nodes.label: Energy supply disruption risk premium
nodes.description: The component of energy prices attributable to market perceptions of disruption risk to supply chains and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Seaborne transport disruption rate
nodes.description: The rate at which maritime cargo movements (especially energy shipments) are delayed, rerouted, interdicted or denied access per unit time.

nodes.label: Undersea infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The level of exposure and fragility of subsea cables, pipelines and related seabed assets to physical attack or accidental damage.

nodes.label: Shipping insurance premium level
nodes.description: The prevailing additional insurance costs (war, hull, route risk) charged for maritime shipments as a continuous market measure.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve release rate
nodes.description: The volumetric rate at which strategic petroleum or fuel reserves are released into markets or logistics networks per unit time.

nodes.label: Alternative energy routing flow
nodes.description: The volume of energy (oil, refined products, gas) reallocated through non-standard routes, storage or suppliers per unit time.

nodes.label: Regional economic spillover intensity
nodes.description: The magnitude and speed at which security shocks transmit to regional economic indicators (trade, markets, investment) as a continuous state.

Asian supply diplomacy and export adjustments
Anthropic IPO as a Stress Test for the AI Investment Boom
AI revenue growth rate
nodes.description: The rate of change in aggregated revenues earned by large commercial AI developers per unit time.

nodes.label: AI operating loss rate
nodes.description: The pace at which operating losses are being incurred across the AI developer sector per unit time.

nodes.label: Sector cash runway
nodes.description: The average remaining liquidity expressed in months available to sustain current operations across AI developers without new capital.

nodes.label: Capital raising flow
nodes.description: The volume of new external financing (equity, debt, IPOs, private rounds) entering the AI developer sector per unit time.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: The prevailing willingness of investors to accept valuation and operational risk in AI-focused investments.

nodes.label: Market valuation expectations
nodes.description: The expected multiples and overall valuation benchmarks that investors assign to AI companies.

nodes.label: Cloud compute utilization %
nodes.description: The percentage of available cloud and datacentre compute capacity actively consumed by AI training and inference workloads.

nodes.label: Cloud pricing level
nodes.description: The average price charged for unit compute and related cloud services used in AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Compute supply growth
nodes.description: The rate at which specialized compute hardware and effective compute capacity available to AI developers is expanding.

nodes.label: AI safety incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency of model-safety or systems-level incidents (malfunctions, unsafe outputs, containment failures) reported or detected per unit time.

nodes.label: Security vulnerability disclosure rate
nodes.description: The rate at which security vulnerabilities and breaches affecting AI systems and supporting infrastructure are disclosed.

nodes.label: AI talent availability
nodes.description: The supply of qualified engineers, researchers and specialists available to work on advanced commercial AI projects.

nodes.label: Enterprise adoption rate
nodes.description: The rate at which enterprises deploy commercial AI solutions and sign recurring contracts with AI providers per unit time.

nodes.label: Infrastructure credit stress
nodes.description: The degree of financing strain and credit risk affecting providers and operators of cloud, datacentre and related infrastructure.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny
nodes.description: The intensity of regulatory oversight, investigatory activity and policy attention focused on AI development, safety and financial practices.

nodes.label: Equity market liquidity
nodes.description: The depth and ease of trading in public equity markets for technology and AI-related securities, measured by spreads, volumes and price impact.

nodes.label: Regulatory and disclosure fallout from S‑1 revelations
Near-term demand boost for cloud partners
Mounting infrastructure credit stress for neoclouds
Market repricing after detailed prospectus disclosures
Energy-driven market volatility and sector rotation
Energy price level
nodes.description: The aggregated market price level of energy commodities (broadly capturing oil, gas and other fuels) measured on a continuous index scale.

nodes.label: Energy price volatility
nodes.description: The short- to medium-term variability of energy commodity prices, measured as continuous price dispersion or realized/implied volatility.

nodes.label: AI-driven power demand
nodes.description: The evolving rate of electricity consumption attributable to large-scale computing and AI workloads, measured as a continuous growth/process variable.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market and public expectation of future inflation measured on a continuous forecast horizon (e.g., 1–5 year expected inflation).

nodes.label: Monetary policy stance
nodes.description: The prevailing tightness or looseness of monetary policy as reflected by expected policy leanings and communication, represented on a continuous scale.

nodes.label: Real interest rate level
nodes.description: The inflation-adjusted interest rate environment (real yields) across relevant maturities, measured continuously.

nodes.label: Equity market volatility
nodes.description: The market-wide variability of equity prices (aggregate volatility index or realized volatility) measured continuously.

nodes.label: Sector rotation rate
nodes.description: The pace at which capital reallocates between equity sectors (relative weight changes across sectors) measured as a continuous flow/process metric.

nodes.label: Flows to safe assets
nodes.description: The net rate of capital moving into perceived safe-haven asset classes (e.g., sovereign debt, gold, cash equivalents) measured continuously as net flows.

nodes.label: Sector valuation gap
nodes.description: The cross-sectional difference in valuation multiples between advantaged and disadvantaged sectors, measured as a continuous spread.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: The aggregate willingness of investors to accept risk for return, measured as a continuous sentiment/behavioral index.

nodes.label: Retail equity flow
nodes.description: The net rate of retail investor capital entering or exiting equity markets, measured continuously as flow volume or proportion.

nodes.label: Hedge fund leverage
nodes.description: The aggregated leverage exposure of hedge funds and similar active strategies measured as a continuous ratio or level of borrowed/derivative exposure.

nodes.label: Commodity supply disruption risk
nodes.description: The assessed probability and magnitude of supply-side disruptions across key commodities (energy, metals) measured as a continuous risk index.

nodes.label: Earnings revision trend
nodes.description: The directional rate at which corporate earnings expectations are being revised up or down across the market, measured as a continuous trend/process.

nodes.label: Currency strength index
nodes.description: The broad value of the reference currency against a basket of peers, measured continuously and capturing currency-driven purchasing power changes.

Public grievance intensity
nodes.description: Aggregate level of population-perceived economic and political grievances driving discontent.

nodes.label: Protest mobilization rate
nodes.description: Speed at which individuals are recruited or mobilized into collective demonstrations and actions.

nodes.label: Protest magnitude
nodes.description: Current aggregated scale of public demonstrations measured by participants, events and geographic spread.

nodes.label: Protest violence level
nodes.description: Prevalence and severity of violent tactics and clashes occurring within protest events.

nodes.label: Election surprise potential
nodes.description: Systemic probability and magnitude of unexpected or contested electoral outcomes altering political balance.

nodes.label: Incumbent legitimacy
nodes.description: Public and elite perception of the political authority and mandate of current officeholders.

nodes.label: Security response intensity
nodes.description: Scale and aggressiveness of policing, security and coercive measures deployed in response to unrest.

nodes.label: Policy concession rate
nodes.description: Speed and magnitude at which authorities implement concessions, reforms or relief measures in response to pressures.

nodes.label: Legal contestation activity
nodes.description: Intensity of judicial, administrative and procedural challenges used to dispute political or electoral outcomes.

nodes.label: Investor capital flow
nodes.description: Net pace and direction of portfolio and capital movements into or out of the domestic market in response to political signals.

nodes.label: Asset price volatility
nodes.description: Degree of short-term variability in key asset prices and exchange rates reflecting market instability.

nodes.label: Investor risk sentiment
nodes.description: Aggregate market perception of political and economic risk influencing risk appetite and portfolio decisions.

nodes.label: Media amplification strength
nodes.description: Rate and intensity with which traditional media frames and spreads information about protests and political events.

nodes.label: Social-media virality
nodes.description: Speed and reach of protest-related content propagation across social platforms and networks.

nodes.label: Cross-border signal transmission
nodes.description: Strength and speed of political, informational and financial shock propagation across national boundaries.

nodes.label: Institutional trust level
nodes.description: Aggregate public confidence in core institutions such as government, judiciary and electoral systems.

Sustained elevated energy prices raise the marginal cost of compute and data-centre operations, forcing higher customer prices or margin compression that slows revenue growth for large commercial AI providers.

Sharp swings in energy prices force frequent revaluation of energy-linked corporate earnings and hedging positions, driving higher short-term volatility across equities, bonds and FX as markets rebalance.

Sharp short-term swings in energy prices increase incentives for state and proxy actors to conduct demonstrative or coercive cross-border strikes (against shipping, facilities or bases) to influence market sentiment or signal resolve, raising strike frequency.

Acute volatility in energy prices induces a market-wide risk-off, tightens liquidity and underwriting terms, and prompts investors to delay or withdraw from new equity/debt deals, immediately reducing capital raising for AI developers.

A decline in investor risk appetite reduces capital for upstream energy projects and raises insurance/finance costs for shipping and infrastructure, which markets translate into a higher energy supply-disruption risk premium.

A decline in investor appetite reduces capital available for satellite launches, constellation maintenance and capacity expansion, causing delays or cuts in commercial satcom coverage and throughput in the conflict theatre.

Material risks to commodity supplies trigger export controls, rerouting of trade and emergency diplomacy that rapidly transmit political and economic shocks and signals across neighboring and linked states.

Persistent or visible failures to secure key commodity supplies undermine public perceptions of government competence and regulatory capacity, eroding trust in core institutions over subsequent months.

Rising assessed commodity supply-disruption risk prompts shipping companies, insurers and naval actors to reroute, delay or interdict voyages and for states to escalate maritime interdiction/escorting operations, directly increasing the observed rate of seaborne transport disruptions.

Disruptions in energy and critical metal supplies constrain manufacturing, launch cadence and ground‑station upkeep for commercial satcom providers, reducing available bandwidth and coverage in the theatre.

Rising risk of supply disruptions for energy and critical materials drives governments to expand national-security reviews, tighten export controls and foreign-investment screening, increasing regulatory oversight of AI firms and their supply chains.

Large, sustained protests physically block or disable extraction, processing and transport infrastructure (ports, pipelines, refineries) and trigger labor stoppages, directly increasing the assessed probability and magnitude of supply disruptions.

Large-scale protests in neighboring states degrade local security posture and tie down government forces, creating permissive windows that Iranian-aligned militias exploit to increase the frequency of cross‑border strikes.

Spikes in asset-price volatility trigger margin calls and rapid portfolio rebalancing that force large, abrupt flows into or out of energy futures and physical markets, amplifying realized and implied energy price volatility.

Spikes in asset-price volatility cause operators and service providers to defer nonessential expenditures and staffing, degrading patching, monitoring and resilience measures and increasing susceptibility of commercial comms to interception, spoofing or jamming.

Spikes in asset-price volatility raise the effective cost of capital and close IPO/secondary windows, causing venture and public capital-raising for AI firms to pause or shrink until markets stabilize.

Deteriorating investor risk sentiment tied to geopolitical realignment causes traders and funds to widen risk premia on energy contracts, directly raising the market component priced as disruption risk for supply chains in the region.

Improved investor risk sentiment lowers financing costs and unlocks capital for satellite launches, ground infrastructure and capacity leases, increasing available commercial satcom bandwidth and coverage serving the theatre.

An improvement (or deterioration) in investor risk sentiment directly changes portfolio allocations for AI sectors—better sentiment causes allocators to accept higher valuation and operational risk in AI investments while worse sentiment causes immediate de-risking.

Faster and stronger cross-border transmission of political and regulatory shocks (sanctions, export controls, border closures) causes secondary supplier interruptions and logistical cascades that raise commodity supply disruption risk.

Faster, stronger cross-border signal transmission (communications, targeting data and logistics channels) directly enables Iranian command-and-control and proxy networks to coordinate and time more frequent long‑range strikes across borders.

Enhanced cross‑border signalling accelerates coordination of maritime harassment, interdiction and information operations by state and proxy actors (targeting routes, flag states or ports), directly increasing rates of seaborne transport disruption.

Faster and stronger cross-border transmission of political information and coordination prompts states to implement targeted technical and policy restrictions (throttling, geofencing, targeted shutdowns) to blunt spillovers into the Russia–Ukraine theatre.

Faster and stronger cross-border transmission of political, information or financial shocks leads governments to impose export controls, data/localization rules and additional compliance checks on cross-border AI activity, increasing regulatory scrutiny.

A marked decline in institutional trust precipitates policy paralysis, regulatory flip-flops or elevated risk of resource seizures that reduce effective supply or add a sustained risk premium, lifting energy price levels.

Declines in public trust in institutions incentivize governments to exert more formal and informal pressure on private communications providers to control narratives and limit disruptive content related to the conflict.

Falling institutional trust prompts legislators and regulators to open investigations and introduce tighter oversight of prominent AI developers to restore public confidence, whereas rising trust reduces political pressure for new scrutiny.
